about: Mechanic Intersectionality Tool data for Dotburg. Hand-kept: add a mechanic, link or idea here, then republish the page (claude/mechanics-page.html). A link means the player can SEE mechanic 'from' change mechanic 'to' (code links with no visible effect do not count). Direct effects only. Levels: 1 flavor (a cosmetic touch), 2 nudge (changes odds or choices), 3 drives (B depends on A). Ideas are proposed links, not built. Checked against CLAUDE.md and the code notes Nov 11 (0.45), not yet line by line.

mechanics.name: Growth
mechanics.summary: Own clock gives one unit per 20 s; units become newcomers, buildings, upgrades and tiers up to City.

mechanics.name: Construction
mechanics.summary: Scaffolding and builders over a lot while something is built or upgraded.

mechanics.name: Dot-men
mechanics.summary: Homes, visits, night owls, stable ids and habits; the people the rest acts on.

mechanics.name: Crier and chronicle
mechanics.summary: The news, as toasts over the town picture (0.52; the crier box is gone), and the file of major events.

mechanics.name: Day and night
mechanics.summary: Six-minute day: lights, sleep, curfew hours, the clock politics and events roll on.

mechanics.name: Seasons
mechanics.summary: Four seasons of four days; palettes, mood drift, illness timing.

mechanics.name: Weather
mechanics.summary: Markov sky by scheme and season: clouds, rain, snow cover, fog, storms, lightning flash.

mechanics.name: Small life
mechanics.summary: Smoke, cat, ducks, fireflies, birds, aurora. Cosmetic.

mechanics.name: Rule
mechanics.summary: Nine rules chosen on becoming a Village; costs, home bonus, curfew, guards, banner.

mechanics.name: Leader and traits
mechanics.summary: A leader dot-man with two of eight traits, epithets, heirs, statues.

mechanics.name: Mood
mechanics.summary: The town's mood bar, pulled by season, crowding, illness, festivals and the leader.

mechanics.name: Politics
mechanics.summary: Every quarter day: revolution, coup, assassination, elections, reforms, emigration, arrests.

mechanics.name: Guards and curfew
mechanics.summary: Patrols, escorts, curfew, rallies under harsh rule.

mechanics.name: Festivals
mechanics.summary: Bunting and dancing after a finished public building or a tier-up.

mechanics.name: Illness
mechanics.summary: Five illnesses, spread by shared building, severity racing immunity, care and quarantine.

mechanics.name: Weddings and births
mechanics.summary: Weddings owe a baby; children drawn lighter for a day, extra to the cap.

mechanics.name: Fires
mechanics.summary: RimWorld-style: a fire has a size that grows on fuel and shrinks under rain, water and fighters; it eats the building, may jump to flammable neighbours, and leaves a ruin rebuilt after a day or two.

mechanics.name: Treasury
mechanics.summary: Gold from caravans and aid; paid out in pleas, pacts and tribute.

mechanics.name: Sister towns
mechanics.summary: Charter, relations, envoys, letters, aid, pacts, quarrels, absorption and collapse.

mechanics.name: Migration
mechanics.summary: Newcomers and emigrants carry a colour to and from named sisters; refugees, exiles.

mechanics.name: Visitors
mechanics.summary: Envoys, trade teams, spies, caravans: not citizens, not saved.

mechanics.name: War
mechanics.summary: This town and a sister fight for one to three days: soldiers march out of the west gate, news comes from the front, raiders may set a building alight; the harsher, bigger side usually wins. Two sisters can also fight (news only).

mechanics.name: Plague and famine
mechanics.summary: One plague or famine at a time starts in a random town of the region and creeps from town to town for three to six days. Sisters lose people; here plague becomes the grey plague outbreak and famine means dear goods, hunger deaths and leavers.

mechanics.name: Messenger
mechanics.summary: MSN-style panel in place of the chronicle: our leader as "me", sisters, group chats between sisters and notables (captain, physician, warden, ringleader) as contacts with status and personal messages; read only, emoticons, typing delay, nudge on urgent news. Last 40 lines per chat saved.

links.why: Units become newcomers who walk in at the west gate and take the emptiest home.
Each building or upgrade starts scaffolding on its lot.
Becoming a Village makes the town choose its rule.
Rule cost multiplier and home bonus change unit cost and population cap.
A finished public building or a tier-up triggers a festival.
A finished City is chartered as a sister and a new hamlet is founded.
A town at its population cap is a little less content.
Crowding raises the odds of an outbreak.
Deaths and leavers open places, so newcomers fill them again.
Builders appear on scaffolding.
Dot-men sleep at night; night owls and curfew change who is out.
Politics and events roll once per quarter day.
Fireflies and the aurora come out at night.
Incubation, severity and immunity run in days.
Sky odds and snow cover depend on the season.
Each season nudges mood up or down.
Each illness has the seasons it favours.
Snow, ducks and birds follow the season.
Storms keep people indoors; nobody sits in the park in the rain.
Rain, snow and fog change what the small life does.
Weather changes are announced.
The rule sets the title, term, succession and which traits are likely.
Each rule has its own baseline mood.
Harsh rules have curfew, guards and rallies.
Harshness sets the odds of revolt, coup, arrest and emigration.
Harsh rule seals sick houses: less spread, lower mood.
The festival line and look follow the rule.
Rules that differ in harshness quarrel; similar ones sign agreements.
Traits move the mood level.
Traits change assassination, revolt, coup, arrest, scandal and emigration odds.
Merciful and able leaders raise care for the sick; a Cruel one seals houses.
Traits change income.
The leader lives at the seat and wears a gold pixel; proud leaders get statues.
Anger makes revolt possible; unrest drives emigration.
Unhappy dot-men leave town.
Content towns marry more.
Revolutions, coups and reforms change the rule.
Deaths, elections, step downs and coups change who leads.
Events dip or lift mood.
Arrests, exiles and emigrants leave; escorts walk.
Emigrants and exiles join a named sister.
Each turn of events is announced and the big ones chronicled.
Curfew and rallies press on mood.
Curfew sends people home early; guards patrol the roads.
Dot-men join the dancing under bunting.
A festival lifts spirits.
The sick go home to bed, tinted by the illness; some die.
Sickness drags mood down.
A leader can die of it.
The first visible case is announced and the toll chronicled.
Illness spreads between dot-men who share a building.
Adults marry and are the parents of children.
A baby is a new dot-man, lighter until grown, extra to the cap.
A letter from a friendly sister can propose a wedding.
Gold buys aid, pacts and tribute, and moves relations.
A fuller treasury draws more caravans.
Envoys, teams, spies and caravans come from sisters, drawn by attitude.
Caravans and fairs earn gold.
Newcomers arrive from, and leavers settle in, named sisters.
Migrants and refugees change the town colours and headcount.
Letters, pacts and quarrels are announced.
Rain cuts a fire down and puts it out in seconds; snow cover and a dry spell change how likely and how fierce.
Summer and dry spells raise the odds of a kitchen fire; winter hearths a little.
Dot-men run out, rush to the blaze with buckets (a blue pixel), and sleepers may be caught inside.
More dot-men at the blaze means more water on it; a small town has too few and loses the building.
A burnt lot becomes a ruin, then is rebuilt through scaffolding.
A Town gets a fire brigade; wells and fountains next door help; bigger towns have more neighbours to catch fire.
Live fires and ruins weigh on mood; a burn-down dips it.
A building lost costs gold; a rich town rebuilds faster, a poor one slower.
Harsh rule blames a saboteur and arrests; commune and council take a collection; a guild rebuilds in half the time.
A harsh state turns a fire into an arrest.
A leader can perish in a fire.
Alarm, spread, rain, bucket line and burn-down lines; burn-downs are chronicled.
A saboteur from a sister can start one.
Spies sent by a sister may turn out to be saboteurs.
Flames glow brighter at night, and fewer people are awake to fight them.
The harsher the rule (and the harsher its neighbours), the likelier it picks a fight.
Every war is against a named sister; the war moves her relation, and she shrinks when she loses.
A beaten sister loses a fifth of her people and may change rule; relations fall; struck sisters lose gold and may be sent aid.
Soldiers march out of the west gate; some never come home, the rest walk back in.
War presses on mood, except under harsh rule that thrives on it; victory lifts it, defeat sinks it.
A war costs gold every quarter day; victory brings plunder, defeat a bill.
Raiders from the foe set a building alight.
A lost war can topple a harsh ruler by revolution, or hand a gentle town to its army.
Victory is celebrated with a festival.
No envoys, teams or caravans come while the war lasts.
When one sister overruns another, refugees reach the gate: taken in or turned back.
Marches, black-edged letters, victory and defeat are announced and chronicled.
Plague reaching the town starts the grey plague outbreak.
Famine kills by hunger and sends people away.
In a famine everything costs a third more.
A famine drags the town down.
Stricken sisters lose people and gold, may need aid, and the weakest can collapse.
No caravans travel in a plague or famine.
Each new town it reaches is announced.
Plague favours winter; famine favours hard winters and dry spells.
A wet sky raises the odds of plague; a long dry spell raises the odds of famine.
It starts in any town of the region and spreads from sister to sister, so it can reach us from outside.
Rain or snow puts a festival off until the sky clears and breaks up one already under way; a ruler's rally goes ahead regardless.

Each sister is a contact: her status comes from relations, war and blight (Busy, Away, Blocked), and she writes about envoys, letters, fairs, spies, caravans, wars and her own revolutions; she signs in when founded and off when absorbed or collapsed.
The captain reports from the front; a declared war nudges the panel; sisters at war show Busy and quarrel in group chats.
The physician writes when an outbreak starts and when it passes; plague nudges the panel; our status turns Busy.
The warden writes at each fire, put-out, burn-down and death; a great fire nudges the panel.
A sister in a blight shows Away and writes about plague or famine.
Our leader answers gently or harshly by the rule (0.6 and up is harsh); each rule has a motto as a personal message.
Under harsh rule a ringleader contact grumbles, mourns arrests and cheers a revolution, then retires.
The leader is the signed-in "me": name, display picture and the reply voice.
A friendly sister congratulates us on each new tier.
Crier lines pop up as toasts; a chat line in the same moment replaces the crier toast; the Chronicle is a contact.

ideas.idea: A festival crowd is a shared room: it spreads illness; a festival could be called off in an outbreak.
A monarch heir is a child born in town and takes the throne when grown.
A school makes children grow up sooner.
A sick migrant or caravan carries illness to or from a sister.
Floods hit low lots in spring and a poor harvest slows growth (famine already makes everything dearer).
Idle crier chatter that reflects the leader traits.
A travelling hero beats back the flames (the mod did this).
Burnt-out families crowd into other homes, so illness spreads faster after a fire.
Soldiers away mean fewer weddings; a victory brings a crop of babies.
A junta or party state sends more soldiers than a council can.
A festival is called off in a plague or famine; a harvest festival ends one.
A festival in good weather lasts longer and draws bigger crowds.
Reply buttons: choose the answer to a plea, tribute demand or wedding offer, changing relations and gold (turned down for 0.52, the owner chose read only).

onPurpose.why: Small life stays cosmetic by design: it makes the town look alive and changes nothing.
The crier is a mirror of what happened, not a mechanic that acts.
